title: The Workout That Burns Fat but Spares Muscle
hook: In adults in their 70s, only high-intensity intervals trimmed body fat while holding onto the muscle that keeps you strong and independent.
key_points: Six-month study of more than 120 adults in their 70s compared exercise intensities.
High-intensity interval training (HIIT) cut body fat while preserving muscle mass.
Moderate and low-intensity workouts trimmed some fat but didn't protect muscle as well.
Holding onto muscle matters more with age — it underpins strength and independence.
Short bursts of hard effort, not just steady cardio, may be the edge for older adults.
content_html: Losing weight in later life comes with a hidden risk: a slimmed-down number on the scale can mean losing muscle along with fat, and muscle is exactly what older adults can least afford to give up. A six-month study of more than 120 adults in their 70s, reported by ScienceDaily, looked at which kind of exercise avoids that trap.
extra_html:
The standout was high-intensity interval training — short bursts of vigorous effort alternated with recovery. While moderate and low-intensity workouts also produced some fat loss, only HIIT reduced body fat while preserving lean muscle. That distinction matters, because muscle is the foundation of strength, balance, and the ability to keep doing everyday tasks independently — and it grows harder to maintain with age.

The result doesn't mean older adults should leap straight into all-out sprints. Intensity is relative, and the sensible path is to build up gradually and check with a clinician before starting something new, especially with existing health conditions. But it does push back on the idea that gentle, steady movement is automatically the safest choice for aging bodies: a bit of hard effort, done sensibly, may be what protects the muscle that keeps you on your feet.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: The Strength-Training Sweet Spot for a Longer Life
related.hook: A 30-year study of 147,000 people points to a modest target: about 90–120 minutes of strength training a week was linked to the biggest drop in risk of dying.

related.title: Why Strength Training Matters
related.hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.

flashcards.prompt: In the study of adults in their 70s, what set high-intensity interval training (HIIT) apart?

choices.text: It reduced body fat while preserving muscle mass
It was the only workout that built no fitness at all
It caused more fat gain than other workouts

flashcards.explanation_html: Moderate and low-intensity exercise also trimmed some fat, but only HIIT preserved lean muscle while reducing body fat.

flashcards.prompt: Why is preserving muscle, not just losing fat, so important with age?
flashcards.back_html: Muscle underpins strength and independence, and it becomes harder to keep as we age. A workout that sheds fat and spares muscle protects the ability to do everyday tasks.
